name: cap-memory-use
description: How to use memory as a caller: write one claim at one scope with an expiry, recall at a scope you hold, and act on what comes back with its age attached. The same two calls whether the writer is a person, an agent, or an event arriving from outside. Load it when a step should remember something for next time, when you are about to pass a whole transcript to the next run because there is nowhere else to put what it learned, when a recall came back empty or refused and you need to know which, when a remembered fact turned out to be wrong, or before you add a cache, a notes file or a table of your own to keep something between runs.

purpose.text: cap-memory states the contract and cap-memory-implement builds it; this facet reduces both to two things a caller does - write one claim, recall at a scope - so remembering across runs is two calls on a step rather than a store you own.
purpose.quote: It has to be simple to use.

operations.name: remember (the whole of what a step writes)
operations.input: scope, one claim, and an expiry - and nothing else; the provenance, the correlation id and the actor come from the run you are already in (proposed)
operations.output: a memory_id. You do not choose an index, an embedding or a key format (proposed)

operations.name: recall (the whole of what a step reads)
operations.input: a scope selector naming at least one dimension you hold, your need in words or an explicit key, and a limit (proposed)
operations.output: items with their provenance and their age, plus the scope that was applied; zero items is a normal answer, not a failure (proposed)

shapes.name: Worked example 1 (proposed): a person's run remembers, an agent's later run recalls - TARGET T1's first two ways in

schema.title: One claim written in run A, recalled in run B by something else
schema.description: Only the produced_by subject differs between a human-initiated write and an agent's. Neither writer named an index, and the reader named a scope and a need.

body.claim: Release notes for this repo are reviewed by the release-reviewer agent before publication, not by the author.
Coupon pricing tests need the tier fixture loaded first; without it they fail on a missing key rather than on the change under test.

query.need: anything to know before running the pricing tests

shapes.name: Worked example 2 (proposed): an event and a schedule reach the same two calls - TARGET T1's third way in

schema.title: Nothing about the calls changes when no person is present
schema.description: An external event writes what it observed, and a scheduled run recalls at the same scope the next morning. The subject prefix is the only difference from example 1.

body.claim: The nightly index rebuild failed twice this week on the same shard; the retry succeeded both times.

query.need: recent failures on the nightly rebuild

shapes.name: The failure shape (proposed): a recall at a scope the caller does not hold

schema.title: The scope is not yours
schema.description: Media type application/problem+json. This is not the same as an empty result: empty means nothing was learned at a scope you hold, denied means you asked at a scope you do not.

examples.title: The scope is not yours
examples.detail: recall named principal user:dana; the run's actor is user:corey and holds principal user:corey, agent agent:release-reviewer and org org:platform.

invariants.text: You never choose how an item is found. cap-memory keeps ranking out of the contract, and the consequence for a caller is that there is no index, no threshold and no k to tune: if a recall returns the wrong things, the fix is a narrower scope or a clearer claim, never a retrieval parameter.
invariants.quote: rank candidate memories by cosine similarity

invariants.text: The three ways in are the same two calls. TARGET T1 names a human, an agent, and an internal or external event as the ways into the system; here all three write and recall the same shapes, differing only in the produced_by subject - user:, agent:, service: or schedule: - and the platform records which one it was. This is the one enumeration of ways in used in this skill.
invariants.quote: An internal or external event must be able to enter the system.

invariants.text: Enhancing one aspect leaves the rest untouched: composability allows enhancing particular aspects of any element without touching the rest. Swap the store cap-memory-implement binds, add decay to ranking, tighten the retention defaults, and no step that remembers or recalls is edited - a scope, a claim, an expiry and a need are the only things any of them named.
invariants.quote: Composability allows enhancing particular aspects of any element without touching the rest.

invariants.text: Everything you write expires, and you say when. cap-memory requires a staleness policy on every write, so the question a caller answers at write time is not whether this should be forgotten but when - and a claim you would not defend in three months gets three months, not a pin.
invariants.quote: raw episodic data should always carry one

invariants.text: Empty and refused are different answers. cap-errors owns the closed registry of RFC 9457 problem details and cap-memory requires refusals to be typed; as a caller you read type first, then retryable, and you never treat a denied scope or an unreachable store as 'nothing learned'.

instructions.action: Write one claim per item, in a sentence a later run can act on, at the narrowest scope that will need it. Do not paste the conversation it came from.
instructions.why: cap-memory cites the prior art that memory exists so work can carry across turns, sessions, and tasks; the caller-side consequence is that a pasted transcript pushes the summarising onto every future reader and expires as one block instead of per fact. Narrow first also means an item can be promoted to a wider scope later, while a wide one cannot be un-shared.
instructions.quote: remember information across turns, sessions, and tasks

instructions.action: Give every write an expiry you would actually accept, or mark it for review with a date. If you cannot name either, the item is not worth writing.
instructions.why: cap-memory requires the policy at write time precisely so it is not decided by whoever cleans up later. A store with no temporal validity model with no expiry dates or conflict detection is how a run acts confidently on last quarter's arrangement.
instructions.quote: no temporal validity model with no expiry dates or conflict detection

instructions.action: Recall with a scope you hold and your need in words, then act on the items and their ages. Treat zero items as the normal answer on a first run, and continue.
instructions.why: The scope selector is what keeps another principal's items out of your context, and the age is what lets you, as cap-memory's step 5 requires of the interface, note this staleness rather than presenting the information as current. A caller that treats an empty recall as an error makes every first run look broken.
instructions.quote: note this staleness rather than presenting the information as current

instructions.action: When something you remembered turns out to be wrong, supersede it with the corrected claim. Never write a second item that contradicts the first, and never edit in place.
instructions.why: cap-memory makes supersession the correction path so contradictions never accumulate; two live items that disagree turn every later recall into a coin toss, and the run that gets the wrong one has no way to tell.
instructions.quote: active supersession on every write so contradictions never accumulate

instructions.action: Never write a grading criterion, a rubric, a secret or another principal's data into an item. If a judge needs to remember its criterion, it writes at its own scope.
instructions.why: agentic-stack states design rule 6 (F-b1-07); recall puts items straight into an agent's context, so an item is the shortest path there is from a criterion to the thing being judged by it.
instructions.quote: An agent sees its outcome, never the criterion it is judged against

instructions.action: Read a refusal as a problem-details object: check type, then retryable, then act on detail. A denied scope is fixed by asking at a scope you hold; an unavailable store is not fixed by asking again with different words.
instructions.why: Proposed usage of the failure shape above. The three refusals a caller actually meets are a denied scope, a write with no staleness policy, and an unreachable store, and only the last is ever worth a retry.

instructions.action: Do not build a notes file, a cache or a table of your own to carry something between runs. If the store you need does not exist, add it as an adapter behind this interface and read cap-memory-implement's binding record and conformance run.
instructions.why: A private store is a second place facts live, with its own scope rules, its own expiry (usually none) and nothing wired to policy or provenance. It cannot be daunting or overly complex, or no one will use it - which cuts both ways: two calls everyone knows beats a store per team that each does a little more.
instructions.quote: It cannot be daunting or overly complex, or no one will use it.

best_practices.text: Proposed: say out loud, in whatever you produce, when you acted on a remembered item and how old it was. The item's age comes back with it, so the cost is one clause, and it is what lets a reader catch a stale arrangement that the run could not.
best_practices.quote: An agent that retrieved a deployment guide last updated eighteen months ago

best_practices.text: Proposed: write at the end of the work, not during it. A claim written mid-run records what you believed then; the same claim written after the outcome is known records what turned out to be true, and only the second is worth recalling.

Proposed: prefer an explicit key when you already know what you are looking for. cap-memory accepts a key as well as a need in words, and an exact key is the one query both stores answer identically - a need in words is answered well by the ranked store and only roughly by the file-backed one.
best_practices.quote: which are tagging dimensions, not nested layers

definition_of_done.criterion: The caller-side half of cap-memory's criterion, proposed tool: `python3 tools/conformance/memory_use.py --writer user:corey --writer agent:release-reviewer --writer service:deploy-webhook --case recall-same-scope --case recall-cross-scope --case recall-expired --report out/memory-use.json`. Each of TARGET T1's three ways in writes one claim in run A; a separate later process runs the three cases against each. It asserts `writers_run == 3`, `recalled_across_runs == 1` per writer on recall-same-scope, `cross_scope_hits == 0`, `expired_served == 0`, `caller_edits == 0` (no calling code differs between writers) and `untyped_refusals == 0`.
definition_of_done.breakage: Give the event writer its own store keyed by the webhook's own identifier instead of writing at the org scope it was handed, changing nothing else, and re-run the same command.
definition_of_done.expected_failure: exit 1 with `recalled_across_runs: 0` for `service:deploy-webhook` while the other two writers still report 1, and `caller_edits: 1` naming the event path. Singling out one writer is the point: a failure that hits all three is a broken fixture, not a broken boundary. Claimed: the tool, the fixtures and both stores do not exist in this tree and no run has been performed, so this check starts red by construction.
definition_of_done.quote: An internal or external event must be able to enter the system.

open_questions.question: Should a caller be able to recall at a scope it holds but did not write at - an agent reading its principal's items - by default, or only when the workflow declares it?
open_questions.evidence: Count, over real runs, how often an agent's useful recall came from its principal's scope rather than its own, against how often a principal's item reached an agent that should not have had it. If the second number is not near zero, the widening belongs in the workflow declaration where a reviewer can see it.
open_questions.default: Proposed: a recall names the dimensions it wants and the platform intersects them with what the actor holds, so reading the principal's scope is allowed but always explicit. An implicit union would make the scope applied to a recall something no caller wrote down.
open_questions.quote: user_id for facts that persist across sessions
